newsitem.title: USA: Cohen urges South Korea not to buy Russian missiles.
newsitem.headline: Cohen urges South Korea not to buy Russian missiles.

text.p: U.S. Defense Secretary William Cohen on Saturday urged South Korea not to buy Russian SA-12 anti-aircraft missiles, suggesting they might accidentally threaten friendly U.S. jets in the confusion of any new Korean war.

Cohen warned at the start of a week-long trip that will take him to Japan and South Korea that it would be a political and military mistake for U.S. ally Seoul to accept Russia's offer of SA-12s instead of buying American Patriot air defense missiles.

"It would not play well in (the U.S.) Congress at all," he told reporters flying with him from Washington to Hawaii for an overnight stop. Cohen said that the missiles were not compatible with U.S. equipment.

"It would not be a good deal, I think, overall ultimately for our relationship. It's important that they stay with U.S. equipment," the secretary said in a pointed response to questions on the controversy.

Cohen also told reporters in an interview aboard his aircraft that he will travel to China this year to press closer military ties with Beijing, but added that 100,000 American troops will remain in the western Pacific area and Asia for the forseeable future.
"I haven't got a definite time yet, but I will be there (China) before the end of the year," he said.

But even if North and South Korea make peace and unite into one state, he said, a U.S. military presence is likely to remain on the Peninsula, where the United States has some 36,000 troops, to keep stability in Asia.

"We believe that it is important to maintain a significant presence for the purpose of promoting stability and we intend to remain in Korea if there is a reunification, into the indefinite future," Cohen said.

Regarding the missiles, Cohen and other U.S. officials voiced concern about "inter-operability" of the SA-12, one of the world's most advanced air defense weapons, with U.S. F-15 and other warplanes based in South Korea to deter any new war with North Korea.

Russia is offering to sell advanced warplanes and other military equipment to many nations around the world and Cohen stressed that Washington could not dictate what its allies could buy. But he said such purchases should be carefully considered.

One senior defense official said privately that Russia was more than $1 billion in debt to Seoul and wanted to provide weapons as partial payment, but the Pentagon worried that the SA-12 did not include electronic safeguards that would prevent it from accidentally threatening U.S. jets.
He said Patriots, made by Raytheon Co, are carefully programmed to recognize friendly forces.
The United States has some Patriot batteries stationed in South Korea. But Seoul has not purchased Patriots for its own use.

"I think that it's important that you have as much inter-operability as possible. If you have Russian equipment and also U.S. equipment it might cause some difficulties as far as connectivity and those types of issues," Cohen told reporters.

"Plus, I think there is a political issue involved ... Obviously I'm sure that the Russians are offering a very good deal and they are looking for any cash that they can get. But there is something more involved than a good deal here."
Asked if he would raise the issue with officials in Seoul, Cohen said simply that "I'm sure it will come up during the course of conversations."
In Hawaii the secretary held talks on Saturday on regional security with Adm. Joseph Prueher, commander of U.S. forces in the Pacific.

Cohen will begin a two-day visit to Japan on Monday and then go to South Korea for two days before winding up his first visit to the region since replacing William Perry as defense secretary two months ago.
